newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Treasuries end up in technically-driven trade.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Treasuries end up in technically-driven trade.

text.p: U.S. Treasuries closed higher in light trade as players looked for bargains in a technical bounce after three days of consecutive losses, analysts said.
The 6-3/4 percent benchmark 30-year Treasury bond ended up 10/32 at 97-6/32. Its yield, which closed Monday's session at the psychologically 7.0 percent level, slid to 6.97 percent.

Pundits spent the day digesting every piece of information -- ranging from weekly retail sales data to fresh supply -- in an effort to find clues on which direction and at what speed the U.S. economy is moving.
Pundits said, however, that the data on Tuesday was not enough to clear the economy's current foggy picture.

"The market is skittish. I don't think anyone has a lot of real confidence to go long here, but by the same token they don't have confidence to go short either," said Paul Kasriel, economist at Northern Trust.
"People are afraid to buy aggressively before a potential Federal Reserve (monetary policy) tightening," he added.
The day began with the release of a 0.2 percent rise in the BTM/Schroders weekly chain store sales index in the week ended August 24.
The data were followed by the release of a surprisingly strong consumer confidence report, which showed a reading of 109.4 in August against a revised 107.0 in July.
The stronger-than-expected report prompted some selling in late morning, when bond prices lost about half a point.
But Treasuries recovered later in the session as players saw some value after long-term rates touched the 7.0 percent level late on Monday.
"There was a dip after consumer confidence but...the technical positions are looking reasonably good for a bounce," said David Sloan, senior economist at consulting firm I.D.E.A.
Analysts said, however, a "somewhat disappointing" auction of two-year notes put a cap on price rises.
The Treasury sold $18.75 billion of two-year notes at 6.17 percent. The bid-to-cover ratio was at 2.23, showing demand for the securities was weaker than some had expected.
The non-competitive bids totalled $1.52 billion.
"The auction results were somewhat disppointing. We expected to see better demand for the two's," said a trader at a foreign investment bank here.
Traders said, however, that foreign central bank buying combined with some hedge fund and retail buying provided "a decent" support to the Treasury sale.

"We had some buying there. It was still a decent auction," the trader said. The market now is gearing up for the Treasury sale of $12.5 billion of five-year notes on Wednesday. Analysts said demand for the securities is uncertain.

Players also took a 0.9 percent rise in the three weeks of August against July in the Lynch, Jones & Ryan Inc Redbook retail sales index. The data did little to move prices, but some analysts saw it as a positive sign.

"They updated their projection for the month each week. The first projection for August was up 1.5 percent. The next one was up 1.2 and this was up 0.9... This means over the last two weeks the survey is showing some softening," Kasriel said.

Analysts said the key August employment report -- due out on September 6 -- is expected to shed some light on the future of the economy and give the market a better indication of how fast the economy is growing.
If the report shows a strong and tight labor market, analysts did not discount the possibility of a hike in interest rates by the Fed as soon as September.
"There is a growing expectation, a growing probability that the September 24th (Federal Open Market Committee) meeting could be the time," Kasriel said.
The three-month Treasury bill closed off two basis points at 5.05 percent. The six-month bill was down one point at 5.14 percent. The year bill down one point at 5.44 percent.

The two-year note closed up 1/32 at 100-5/32, yielding 6.16 percent. The five-year note traded up 3/32 at 100-10/32 to yield 6.55 percent. The ten-year note closed up 5/32 at 101-18/32, yielding 6.78 percent.
